faq.a: It can diagnose malaria, sickle‑cell disease and haematologic malignancies without expensive equipment.
faq.q: Why is a peripheral smear important in low‑resource settings?

faq.a: If the patient has chronic cough, weight loss, night sweats and liver imaging shows granulomas, start while awaiting sputum results.
faq.q: When should I start empiric anti‑TB therapy for suspected hepatic TB?

faq.a: Yes, some herbs contain nephrotoxic or hepatotoxic compounds; ask patients specifically about traditional medicines.

exam: What is the next step after finding a malaria parasite on a peripheral smear in a patient with anaemia? — Start artesunate promptly and assess for haemolysis.
How would you differentiate hepatic TB from viral hepatitis using available tests? — Use chest X‑ray for pulmonary TB signs and hepatitis B serology; liver biopsy if uncertain.

A patient with sickle‑cell disease presents with acute chest pain and a normal ECG; what pathology should you suspect and why? — Acute vaso‑occlusive crisis causing pulmonary infarction; treat with analgesia and oxygen.
Why is NSAID use contraindicated in a patient with suspected acute kidney injury? — NSAIDs reduce prostaglandin‑mediated renal perfusion, worsening renal failure.
What red‑flag sign in a patient with jaundice indicates immediate referral? — Development of encephalopathy or asterixis suggesting hepatic failure.

If a laboratory cannot perform serum ferritin, how can you still assess iron‑deficiency anaemia? — Use a combination of low haemoglobin, low mean corpuscular volume and a positive stool occult blood test.

Explain why a patient with chronic hepatitis B should receive hepatitis B vaccination for household contacts. — Vaccination prevents transmission to susceptible individuals, reducing community disease burden.
When is a liver biopsy essential despite limited pathology services? — When imaging and labs cannot distinguish between malignancy and granulomatous disease, and the result will change management.
ai.title: Human Pathology Overview
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: A concise guide for fourth‑year students on how to think clinically about tissue and laboratory pathology in low‑resource African hospitals. Covers definition, causes, presentation, investigations, red flags, management and common pitfalls.

b: Identify the organ system involved
Correlate history with laboratory patterns
sections.p: Pathology is the study of disease mechanisms seen in tissues, cells and body fluids. Diagnosis combines clinical clues with gross, microscopic and laboratory findings.

b: Use WHO grading for tumours when possible
Apply fibrosis stage (F0‑F4) for liver disease
sections.p: Severity is graded by standard histologic scores (e.g., fibrosis stage, tumor grade) or by clinical staging systems such as TNM for cancers.

b: Infectious agents – malaria, HIV, TB, hepatitis B
Parasitic infestations – schistosomiasis
Genetic disorders – sickle‑cell disease
Autoimmune/immune‑mediated – rheumatic fever
sections.p: In East African settings the most common aetiologies are infections (malaria, HIV, TB, hepatitis B), endemic parasites (schistosomiasis), sickle‑cell disease, rheumatic fever and exposure to herbal toxins.

b: Look for organ‑specific dysfunction
Ask about exposure to endemic infections
sections.p: Patients may present with organ‑specific signs (e.g., jaundice for hepatic pathology, hematuria for renal disease) plus systemic features such as fever, weight loss or anaemia.
Laboratory and imaging tests confirm the pathological process and guide treatment.

t.b: Detect anaemia, leukocytosis or thrombocytopenia; guides infection vs marrow failure
Identifies malaria parasites, sickle cells, blasts; essential when automated counters are unavailable
Assess hepatocellular injury vs cholestasis; if reagents missing, use bedside bilirubin colour chart
Detect schistosome eggs, haematuria, proteinuria; if microscopy unavailable, dip‑stick protein and gross haematuria are useful
Shows TB infiltrates or cardiac enlargement; if X‑ray not available, clinical signs of TB (cough, weight loss) guide empiric therapy
Provides definitive tissue diagnosis; if pathology services are limited, fine‑needle aspirate with tele‑pathology can be used

b: Rapidly falling haemoglobin → hemorrhagic shock
Acute renal failure → oliguria, rising creatinine
Encephalopathy in liver disease → altered consciousness
sections.p: Unrecognised severe pathology can lead to organ failure, sepsis, or death.

b: Antimalarials (artesunate) for malaria‑related haemolysis
Antiretroviral therapy for HIV‑associated lymphomas
Empiric anti‑TB therapy for granulomatous liver disease
Iron supplementation only after confirming iron‑deficiency anaemia
Avoid non‑steroidal anti‑inflammatories in renal pathology
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then provide organ‑supportive care. Choose drugs that are affordable, have a wide safety margin and are available in the formulary.

b: Repeat CBC every 4 weeks after initiating therapy
Vaccinate against hepatitis B and pneumococcus
Educate on safe herbal use and malaria prophylaxis
sections.p: Regular monitoring of blood counts, organ function and infection status prevents relapse and detects drug toxicity.

b: Malaria vs. bacterial sepsis – both cause fever and anaemia; malaria smear distinguishes
Hepatitis B vs. alcoholic liver disease – both raise transaminases; viral serology clarifies
sections.p: Many systemic diseases mimic each other clinically.

b: Bilirubin may be normal in early hepatic necrosis; rely on ALT/AST trends
Peripheral smear may miss low‑density malaria; repeat smear if suspicion remains
sections.p: Certain tests may be falsely normal in early disease or altered by local factors.
